name: Suffix Effect
description: Adding an irrelevant final item after a list can selectively damage memory for the true last items. The extra ending element disrupts the normal recency advantage those items would otherwise have.
design_relevance_note: Mostly relevant to spoken menus, voice assistants, IVR systems, audio alerts, or screen-reader-like sequences where users hear ordered options. It has little direct relevance to ordinary visual interface design.
prevalence_note: Mostly confined to auditory-memory literature and very specific voice/audio interface conversations.

findings.description: Appending an irrelevant final auditory item impaired recall of the true last list items in immediate serial recall, supporting the classic suffix effect and tying it to perceptual grouping/cognitive-streaming mechanisms rather than simple masking alone.
findings.source_title: Capturing the suffix: cognitive streaming in immediate serial recall.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
